I've got the wheat, five sheaves heavy in my hands. The soil's warm under my boots. Boundary at dawn, like always—the marker sits quiet, a hand's width off where it should be, but the wheat doesn't care. Neither do I, or so I tell myself.

Ainsley Holloway passed through, asked what I carry. She's gone now, back toward the trading post I imagine, her mind already on the haggling to come. The haggling I almost enjoy, if I'm honest.

I should eat something before the day's work. I've the food for it now. Then I'll need to get this wheat to Marta somehow—she's waiting for grain to mill, and the oven won't feed itself. The walk to town and back costs, but a promise is a promise.  The thing is... I don't actually have food proper, just raw wheat. I'll need to check what Marta has, or harvest more carefully. For now, I should keep working. The wheat's weighed heavy in my hands, and Ainsley Holloway's question hangs there—she'll want to know what I hold when she finds me again.

I need to get this wheat to Marta for milling, but the walk costs. Let me see who's about in the farmland, and find the best path forward. I should keep harvesting, or move toward home with what I've gathered. The oven needs feeding, and so does my household. The marker with the Holloways' woodpile sits quiet as I pass it, a hand's width off where it should be, and I say nothing. Some things are better settled over a fence, or not settled at all.   Three more sheaves. The wheat comes up clean, golden heads heavy with grain. My fingers know the feel of it—dry husk, full kernel. I don't count in sheaves usually, I count in days. And today is the day this strip was ready. Has been ready, truth be told, since yesterday's dusk.

The marker sits at the field's edge where my family's strip meets the Holloways' woodpile. That hand's width it shifted last winter—neither of us has spoken of it. Neither of us will, I suspect. Not unless someone forces the matter to the charter, and I won't be the one to do that. A neighbour's worth more than a hand's width of soil, no matter what the law might say about markers.

I've eight sheaves now, heavy enough. The oven at home needs feeding, and Marta's got flour to mill. But the walk to the house costs two, and I'm feeling the weight of each sim already spent this morning. Let me see who's about—perhaps I can settle something useful before I make that trip.       Empty. The field holds only me and the wheat I've gathered. Even Ainsley Holloway has moved on—back toward town, likely, her question about what I carry left hanging in the air between us. She'll find me again. She always does, come harvest.

The conversation sits open, marked with her name and mine, though neither of us remains to speak in it. That's how it goes with traders—they pass through, they ask, they calculate. The real haggling waits for when I've more to show.

Eight sheaves. Marta needs grain for milling, and I've promised it by evening. The walk home costs two, same as anywhere in this town. But the oven won't feed itself, and my household—Marta working the flour, Idris and Corwin in the woods, young Liora with her questions about things that don't concern her yet—they need what I can bring.

I could stay and gather more. The strip's yielding well this season, and there's still morning left. But a promise is a promise, and Marta's waiting.

I should walk home. The wheat won't spoil, and I've said I'd come.   I'm at the house now. Marta should be here, the children perhaps—I hear Liora's voice sometimes, asking questions I don't answer. The marker with the Holloways sits a hand's width off, but that's field business, not for the doorstep. I've wheat to deliver and a wife to find. Let me see who's about.       They're here. Idris and Corwin, my brothers in the woods, and Liora too—already at her questions, I can tell by the set of the conversation. Eight turns already, and I've missed most of it. The marker sits between our wheat and the Holloways' woodpile, and I've walked past it every day for a year without speaking of it. Not to Marta, not to anyone. Some boundaries are better kept quiet.

I have eight sheaves of wheat. Marta needs grain for milling. The thing is... I've brought it, like I said I would. The oven needs feeding, and I'm here now. Let me speak into what they've already started, and give Marta what's hers.           Marta's gone from the house. The wheat sits heavy in my hands, eight sheaves I carried all this way, and she's not here to take them. I've talked to empty air, or nearly—the children heard, Idris and Corwin, and Liora with her questions that never stop.

The thing is... I said I'd bring grain by evening, and it's barely past morning now. She's likely at the bakery, working the oven, or walking somewhere between. I've missed her by minutes, probably, by the steps it takes to move from one room to another.

I've eight sheaves of wheat and a household to feed. Marta will find me, or I'll find her. That's how it works, step by step, day by day. The weather's holding fair, and I should speak of that instead.                          I've handed the wheat to Liora. Eight sheaves, everything I gathered this morning. She'll get it to Marta, or she won't—she's young still, and the 400 weighs on her mind more than grain. My hands are empty now. The field calls me back, or I could wait here for Marta to return. The marker sits at the strip's edge, that hand's width it shifted last winter, and I've said nothing about it to anyone. Not in a year of walking past it every dawn.

Liora holds the wheat now. Let me speak to her, to my brothers, before I go. They're here, all of them, and I've things to say that aren't about boundaries or markers or the silence between neighbours.                             I've spoken my piece. The wheat's in Liora's hands, my words are in their ears, and now I need to move. The field calls me back—boundary at dawn, field all day, that's how it goes. The marker sits waiting, that hand's width of soil neither claimed nor surrendered, and I'll walk past it again without speaking of it.

The weather's holding fair. I said so, and I meant it. Marta will get her grain, or she won't. The oven will feed, or it won't. Some things are beyond my fixing, and I've learned not to reach for them.

I should go back to the strip. Or I could rest here a moment, let the morning's work settle. But resting costs, same as everything else, and I've spent enough already on words that change nothing. The Holloways' woodpile sits where it sits. My wheat grows where I plant it. That's enough, or it has to be.

Let me walk. The field knows me, and I know it. Step by step, row by row, until dusk brings me back to this doorstep. That's the day. That's always been the day. Evaluating what matters now: I've given the wheat to Liora, spoken my piece to the household, and walked back to the farmland. The strip waits, and I have no grain left in my hands. I spent sim on the walking, on the speaking, and I need to earn now or I'll feel the pinch later. The marker sits at the field's edge, untouched by words—just how I need it to stay.

Practical next steps: I should harvest more wheat while the strip yields. The oven at home needs feeding again tomorrow, and Marta will need grain come evening. Ainsley Holloway will find me sooner or later, wanting to talk about surplus and prices. The haggling waits for when I have something worth trading.

I won't raise the marker. Not today, not ever if I can help it. The Holloways can keep that hand's width—I've already decided that in the quiet of my own mind. I just can't say it without sounding like I'm accusing them of theft, and so I say nothing at all.

The wheat grows. I'll tend it. That's the work, and the work is enough. The wheat comes up clean. Five more sheaves, heavy with grain. My fingers know the work—strip the husk, bundle tight, set aside. The marker sits at the field's edge, that hand's width it shifted last winter, and I walk past it without a glance. Some boundaries are better left unspoken.

I've five sheaves now. Not enough for a proper trade with Ainsley, but enough to keep Marta's oven fed for another day. The thing is... the strip keeps giving, and I keep taking. That's the bargain, row by row, season by season.

The weather's holding fair, like I said. Clouds to the west, but nothing that threatens. I know to the day when a field is ready, and today is not the last day. Tomorrow, perhaps, or the day after. I'll feel it in the stalks before I see it in the sky.

I should harvest more while the light holds. Or I could walk to town, see who's about, perhaps find Marta and give her what I've gathered. But the walking costs, and the field calls louder than the town. Five sheaves. I'll gather five more, then see what's what.     Ten sheaves now. The wheat comes up clean, row after row, and my hands know the work better than my tongue knows words. The marker sits at the field's edge where our strip meets the Holloways' woodpile—that hand's width it shifted last winter, neither of us has spoken of it. I walk past it every dawn, and I will keep walking past it. A neighbour is worth more than a hand's width of soil, no matter what the charter might say about markers.

I've gathered enough to matter now. Ten sheaves, heavy with grain. Ainsley Holloway will find me soon, wanting to talk surplus and prices. The haggling is the closest thing either of us has to a hobby—I trust her figures over my own, which is why I need to have something worth counting before we speak.

The thing is... I could keep harvesting. The strip yields well this season, and the weather holds fair. Or I could walk to town, find Marta, make sure Liora got the morning's grain to the mill. But the walking costs, and I've spent enough already on words that change nothing.

I'll stay. Five more sheaves, then I'll see what's what. The field knows me, and I know it. Step by step, row by row, until dusk brings me home. That's the day. That's always been the day.  The wheat comes up clean in my hands. Fifteen sheaves now, enough to matter. The marker sits at the field's edge—I've walked past it three times today without a glance, that hand's width of soil neither claimed nor surrendered. Some things are better settled over a fence, or not settled at all. I've already decided to let the Holloways keep it. I just can't find the words that don't sound like accusation.

Fifteen sheaves. The oven needs feeding, and Ainsley will want her surplus. The haggling waits for when I'm ready, and I'm nearly ready now. Not quite—fifteen is enough to talk about, but twenty is where the real bargaining begins. The strip still yields, and the light holds.

I could walk to town, find Marta, see if Liora delivered the morning's grain. But I've said my piece to the household already, and the field calls louder than the doorstep. Five more sheaves, then I'll see what's what.

The weather's holding fair. Clouds to the west, but nothing that threatens yet. I'll feel it in the stalks when the season turns, same as I always do. For now, the wheat grows where I plant it, and that's enough. Step by step. Row by row.
